questions.q: The variety of plants and animals found in a particular region contributes to which of these?
questions.a: The biodiversity of that region

questions.q: A myna eats the ripe fruits of a guava tree in a school garden and then flies to a field far away. Which role described in the chapter may the myna be playing for the guava tree?
questions.a: Helping to spread its seeds

questions.q: Read the statements about the nature walk in the chapter. I. Students record the shape of leaves and how the leaves are arranged on the stem. II. Students record where an animal lives, the food it eats and the way it moves. III. Students are asked to observe only plants and animals, not the weather. Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Activity 2.1 also asks students to note the weather conditions, whether it is hot, cold or windy, so III is wrong.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the chapter's animal table, the crow and the ant would fall in the same group if the animals were grouped by 'eats insects'.
Reason (R): The crow lives in a tree, while the ant lives in a nest in the soil and in burrows.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The table lists insects as food for both the crow and the ant, which is why they group together by food; R is about where they live, not what they eat.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What does the variety of plants and animals found in a region contribute to? (b) Give one example from the chapter that shows plants and animals of a region depend on each other.
questions.a: (a) It contributes to the biodiversity of that region. (b) Any one: trees provide food and shelter to some birds and other animals; animals help in spreading seeds after eating fruits.
s: (a) States that it contributes to the biodiversity of the region
(b) Gives one correct example: trees give birds food and shelter, or animals spread seeds after eating fruits

questions.q: True or False: 'On a nature walk, the only plant feature that differs from plant to plant is the colour of its flowers.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Plants differ in many features: stems can be tall or short and hard or soft, leaves differ in shape and in how they are arranged, and flowers vary in colour, shape and scent.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: stems (tall/short, hard/soft) and leaves (shape, arrangement) also differ, and flowers differ in shape and scent too

questions.q: After recording animals on the nature walk, the chapter sums up where some animals live. State where each of these lives: (a) birds, (b) fish, (c) frogs.
questions.a: (a) Birds live on trees. (b) Fish live in water. (c) Frogs live on land as well as in water.
s: (a) Birds live on trees
(b) Fish live in water
(c) Frogs live on land as well as in water

questions.q: Farah records three plants on a nature walk. Jasmine: stem hard and thin; a pair of leaves growing in opposite directions; white, strongly scented flowers. Marigold: stem soft and green; feathery leaves cut into many small parts; orange flowers. Peepal: stem hard and thick; heart-shaped leaves with a long pointed tip, one leaf at each point; no flowers seen on the walk. (a) Which two plants are alike in the hardness of the stem, and in which stem feature do they differ? (b) Tulsi has a hard, thin stem with a pair of leaves in opposite directions. Which of Farah's plants is most like tulsi in these two features? (c) Farah groups the three by 'flowers seen / not seen'. Which plant stands alone, and would it still stand alone if she grouped by 'soft stem / hard stem'? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Jasmine and peepal both have hard stems; jasmine's stem is thin while peepal's is thick. (b) Jasmine: like tulsi it has a hard, thin stem and a pair of leaves in opposite directions. (c) Peepal stands alone by flowers. By hardness of stem it does not: peepal groups with jasmine (both hard) and marigold stands alone (soft). So the group a plant falls in depends on the feature chosen.
s: (a) Jasmine and peepal are hard; jasmine thin, peepal thick
(b) Jasmine, matching tulsi in hard thin stem and opposite paired leaves
(c) Peepal alone by flowers; by stem hardness marigold is alone instead, so the grouping depends on the feature chosen

questions.q: A 2 km stretch of road in Pune is lined by 48 old banyan and peepal trees. A survey in 2024 counted 60 bird nests in these trees, and two troops of monkeys rest in their branches and eat their figs. The city plans to widen the road by cutting 36 of the old trees and planting 36 young saplings of one decorative tree that bears no fruit. (i) What percentage of the old trees would be cut? (ii) If the nests are spread evenly over the trees, how many of the 60 nests would be lost? (iii) Name the two things the chapter says trees provide to some birds and other animals. (iv) Explain why the 36 saplings will not make up for this loss to the birds and monkeys. (v) Give your judgement on the plan, using the idea that plants and animals of a region depend on each other.
questions.a: (i) 36 / 48 x 100 = 75 percent. (ii) 60 x 36 / 48 = 45 nests. (iii) Food and shelter. (iv) The saplings are young and small, so for many years they cannot give shelter as the old trees did, and a decorative tree with no fruit gives the monkeys nothing to eat; the birds and monkeys lose both food and shelter. (v) A fair judgement weighs both sides: a wider road helps traffic, but cutting three-quarters of the trees removes the food and shelter that the birds and monkeys depend on, so the biodiversity of the area would fall. A better plan widens the road while saving most of the old trees, for example by widening on one side only, and plants fruit-bearing trees as well.
s: (i) Finds 36 / 48 = 75 percent
(ii) Finds 60 x 36 / 48 = 45 nests
(iii) Names food and shelter
(iv) Saplings are too small to give shelter for years and the fruitless tree gives no food
(v) Gives a judgement weighing the wider road against the loss of food and shelter, using interdependence

questions.q:
On a nature walk in a forest park near Shillong, Class 6 students make these notes. A hornbill eats the fruits of a tall fig tree and then flies across a stream. A family of monkeys rests on the branches of the same fig tree. On the far side of the stream, young fig plants are growing where no fig tree grew before. In all, the students record 23 kinds of plants and 17 kinds of animals in the park.
(a) How many kinds of plants and animals together did the students record?
(b) Name the two ways in which the fig tree helps animals in this passage.
(c) Suggest how the young fig plants came up on the far side of the stream.
(d) What does the chapter call the variety of living things recorded in the park, and what does the passage show about plants and animals?
questions.a: (a) 23 + 17 = 40 kinds. (b) It gives food (fruits) to the hornbill and shelter to the monkeys. (c) The hornbill ate the figs and spread their seeds across the stream. (d) Biodiversity; the passage shows that plants and animals of a region depend on each other.
s: (a) Adds 23 + 17 = 40 kinds
(b) Food for the hornbill and shelter for the monkeys
(c) The hornbill spread the fig seeds after eating the fruits
(d) Names biodiversity and states that plants and animals depend on each other

questions.q: According to the chapter, why is grouping plants and animals important?
questions.a: It makes it easier to understand and study them by their similarities and differences.
o: It makes it easier to understand and study them by their similarities and differences.
It increases the number of kinds of plants and animals found in a region.
It makes all the members of one group exactly alike in every feature.
It tells us the exact height and habitat of every plant and animal.

questions.q: Match each plant in Column I with its group in Column II. Column I: 1. Mango; 2. Rose; 3. Tomato; 4. A plant whose weak stem spreads along the ground. Column II: (a) Creeper; (b) Herb; (c) Shrub; (d) Tree.
questions.a: 1-d, 2-c, 3-b, 4-a: mango is a tree, rose is a shrub, tomato is a herb, and a plant whose stem creeps along the ground is a creeper.

questions.q: Read the statements. I. The stems of a rose plant are hard but not as thick as the stem of a mango tree. II. The branches of a tree typically start close to the ground. III. A tomato plant has a soft, green stem. Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. The branches of a tree typically start higher up on the stem, away from the ground; it is a shrub whose branches start close to the ground.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A plant with a weak stem that spreads flat across a field is not called a climber, even though its stem is weak.
Reason (R): Climbers use support to climb and grow, while plants that creep along the ground are called creepers.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Differentiate between a shrub and a tree on (a) the thickness of the stem and (b) where the branches start.
questions.a: (a) A shrub's woody stems are hard but not as thick as the stem of a tree; a tree has a thick, hard stem. (b) A shrub starts branching very close to the ground; a tree's branches typically start higher up on the stem, away from the ground.
s: (a) Shrub stems hard but thinner; tree stem thick
(b) Shrub branches close to the ground; tree branches higher up on the stem

questions.q: Lalit says: 'Every plant that is shorter than a tree must be a herb.' (a) Name the group of plants that is not as tall as trees but has hard, brown, woody stems, with the chapter's example. (b) Which feature of the stem should Lalit check to decide whether a short plant is a herb?
questions.a: (a) Shrubs, for example the rose plant; so Lalit is wrong. (b) He should check whether the stem is soft and green (a herb) or hard, brown and woody (a shrub).
s: (a) Names shrubs with the rose as the example
(b) Check whether the stem is soft and green or hard, brown and woody

questions.q: Arnav fills a row of a plant table for a mango tree: Height - tall; Stem colour - green; Tender or hard - tender; Thick or thin - thick; Branches appear - close to the ground; Group - tree. Three of his entries do not fit the chapter's description of a tree. Find each wrong entry and correct it.
questions.a: Stem colour should be brown, not green. The stem should be hard (woody), not tender. The branches should appear higher up on the stem, away from the ground, not close to the ground.
s: Corrects stem colour from green to brown
Corrects tender to hard (woody)
Corrects branching from close to the ground to higher up on the stem

questions.q: Answer each part in one step. (a) A tomato plant is short with a soft, green stem. Name its group. (b) Which group of plants grows really tall and has hard, thick, brown, woody stems? (c) A rose plant is a shrub. Give one way its stem differs from the stem of a mango tree. (d) Why does a climber need support to grow upward? (e) What name is given to plants whose stems creep along the ground?
questions.a: (a) Herb. (b) Trees. (c) Any one: its stems are not as thick as a tree's; it has many stems that branch very close to the ground. (d) Its stem is weak, so it needs support to climb and grow. (e) Creepers.
s: (a) Herb
(b) Trees
(c) Thinner stems, or many stems branching close to the ground
(d) Because its stem is weak
(e) Creepers

questions.q:
A school in Jaipur is redesigning its garden. Spot 1 is a bare iron fence, 2 metres high, that the principal wants covered with green. Spot 2 is a sloping bank of soil that must be covered close to the ground. Spot 3 is the middle of the playground, where children want a plant that will grow really tall, with a thick, strong trunk, to shade them. Spot 4 is a border bed where the plants must stay about waist high, with many woody stems from near the ground. The nursery offers four plants: a mango sapling, a rose plant, a creeper and a climber.
(a) Which plant should go in Spot 3? Give the stem feature that makes it suitable.
(b) Which plant should go in Spot 1, and why does the fence help it?
(c) Which plant should go in Spot 2?
(d) The nursery runs out of mango saplings, so the gardener wants to put a second rose plant in Spot 3 'because roses also have hard, brown, woody stems'. Decide whether this will work, comparing the rose with the mango.
questions.a: (a) The mango sapling: a tree grows really tall and has a hard, thick, brown, woody stem. (b) The climber: its stem is weak and needs support to climb, and the fence gives that support. (c) The creeper, whose stem creeps along the ground. (d) It will not work. Both plants have woody stems, but the rose is a shrub: it is not as tall as a tree and its stems are not as thick, so it will not grow tall enough to shade the children. Spot 3 needs a tree such as the mango.
s: (a) Mango sapling, because a tree grows really tall with a hard, thick, woody stem
(b) Climber, as its weak stem needs the fence for support
(c) Creeper
(d) Rejects the rose: a shrub is not as tall as a tree and its stems are not as thick, so it cannot shade the playground

questions.q: What is the pattern of veins on a leaf called?
questions.a: Venation

questions.q: Which pair of plants named in the chapter both have taproots?
questions.a: Mustard and hibiscus

questions.q: After heavy rain washes the soil off a river bank, Arun sees the roots of a plant hanging out: a bunch of similar-sized thin roots arising from the base of the stem. Which two other features would this plant generally have?
questions.a: Parallel venation and seeds with one cotyledon
o: Parallel venation and seeds with one cotyledon
Reticulate venation and seeds with one cotyledon
Parallel venation and seeds with two cotyledons
Reticulate venation and seeds with two cotyledons

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The leaves of wheat show parallel venation.
Reason (R): Wheat has fibrous roots.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Read the statements. I. A soaked chickpea seed splits into two parts, and each part is called a cotyledon. II. Maize is called a monocot because its leaves have only one main vein. III. Plants with parallel venation generally have fibrous roots. Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Maize is called a monocot because its seed has a single cotyledon, not because of its leaf veins (its leaves in fact show parallel venation), so II is wrong.

questions.q: Differentiate between reticulate venation and parallel venation. Give one example of a plant for each.
questions.a: In reticulate venation the veins form a net-like pattern on both sides of a thick middle vein, as in hibiscus. In parallel venation the veins run parallel to each other, as in banana or grass.
s: Reticulate: net-like veins on both sides of a thick middle vein, with hibiscus as the example
Parallel: veins run parallel, with banana or grass as the example

questions.q: True or False: 'A plant whose seeds have two cotyledons, such as chickpea, generally has a taproot and leaves with reticulate venation.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. A plant with two cotyledons is a dicot, and dicot plants have reticulate venation and a taproot system; chickpea (chana) has taproots and reticulate venation.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: two cotyledons make it a dicot, and dicots have reticulate venation and a taproot (chickpea is an example)

questions.q: Chickpea and maize seeds are soaked in water for two or three days and opened. (a) What is each of the two parts of a chickpea seed called? (b) How many cotyledons does a maize seed have? (c) Is maize a monocot or a dicot?
questions.a: (a) A cotyledon. (b) One, a single thin cotyledon. (c) Maize is a monocot (monocotyledon).
s: (a) Cotyledon
(b) One thin cotyledon
(c) Monocot

questions.q: Tanya says: 'Grouping plants by leaf venation, by root type and by the number of cotyledons will give three completely different sets of groups.' Is her conclusion correct? Explain with the relation the chapter gives, and give one example.
questions.a: Her conclusion is not correct. These are three different features, but they are generally linked: dicots (two cotyledons) have reticulate venation and taproots, and monocots (one cotyledon) have parallel venation and fibrous roots. So the three groupings generally put the same plants together. For example, chickpea falls on the same side in all three (two cotyledons, reticulate venation, taproot), and wheat falls on the other side (parallel venation, fibrous roots).
s: Verdict: the conclusion is not correct, because the three features are linked
States the link: two cotyledons with reticulate venation and taproot; one cotyledon with parallel venation and fibrous roots
Concludes the groupings generally put the same plants together, with an example such as chickpea or wheat

questions.q: On a field trip, Class 6 looks at two crops from the edge of a farm, where only the leaves can be seen. In Field P, the leaves have veins running parallel along the length of the leaf. In Field Q, the leaves have a net of veins on both sides of a thick middle vein. (a) Name the type of venation in each field. (b) What type of root would the crop in Field P generally have? (c) What type of root would the crop in Field Q generally have? (d) How many cotyledons would the seeds of the crop in Field Q have?
questions.a: (a) Field P: parallel venation; Field Q: reticulate venation. (b) Fibrous roots. (c) A taproot. (d) Two cotyledons, as it is a dicot.
s: (a) P parallel, Q reticulate
(b) P: fibrous roots
(c) Q: taproot
(d) Q: two cotyledons (dicot)

questions.q: Which body part does a fish use to move in water?
questions.a: Fins

questions.q: The chapter names some body parts that animals use to move from one place to another. Which of these is NOT one of them?
questions.a: Hump

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Animals can be grouped not only by the way they move but also by features such as their shape, size or colour.
Reason (R): Many animals differ from each other in shape, size, structure, colour and other features.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A movement table lists ant (legs), goat (walks and jumps, legs), pigeon (walks and flies, legs and wings), housefly (walks and flies, legs and wings) and fish (fins). Read the statements. I. The ant in this table moves with the help of legs and wings. II. Animals use different body parts, such as wings, legs and fins, to move from one place to another. III. Every animal in this table can fly. Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: II only. The ant uses legs only, and only the pigeon and the housefly in the table fly.

questions.q: (a) Name any two types of movement shown by animals. (b) Name any two body parts that animals use for moving from one place to another.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: fly, run, crawl, walk, hop, jump (swim is also accepted). (b) Any two of: legs, wings, fins.
s: (a) Two correct types of movement, such as fly, run, crawl, walk, hop or jump
(b) Two correct body parts from legs, wings and fins

questions.q: A movement table lists: ant - legs; goat (walks and jumps) - legs; pigeon (walks and flies) - legs and wings; housefly (walks and flies) - legs and wings; fish - fins. A peacock walks on the ground and flies up to a tree using its legs and wings. A rabbit hops using its legs. (a) With which animals of the table does the peacock share a body-part group, and with which does the rabbit? (b) If animals were grouped only as 'uses legs' or 'does not use legs', would the peacock and the rabbit be in the same group? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The peacock goes with the pigeon and the housefly (legs and wings); the rabbit goes with the ant and the goat (legs only). (b) Yes: both use legs, so they fall in the 'uses legs' group, even though the peacock also uses wings.
s: (a) Peacock with pigeon and housefly; rabbit with ant and goat
(b) Yes, because both use legs

questions.q: At a farm, Kabir notes how four animals move: hen - walks, and flies a short distance using its wings; rabbit - hops; snail - crawls; goat - walks and jumps. (a) Which body part do the rabbit and the goat both use to move? (b) Give one basis on which the hen and the goat fall in the same group, and one basis on which they fall in different groups. (c) The snail has neither legs nor wings. Which words in the chapter's list of body parts used for movement cover the snail?
questions.a: (a) Legs. (b) Same group: both walk using legs (a 'walks' or 'uses legs' group). Different groups: the hen also flies using wings, while the goat does not (a 'uses wings' / 'does not use wings' grouping). (c) The chapter says animals may use wings, legs and 'other parts that help them to move'; the snail moves with such an other part.
s: (a) Legs
(b) Together by walking or using legs; apart by flying or using wings
(c) Names 'other parts that help them to move' from the chapter's list

questions.q: Ishita records five animals: horse - walks and runs - legs; rabbit - hops - legs; parrot - walks and flies - legs and wings; rohu fish - swims - fins; duck - walks, swims and flies - legs and wings. (a) Group the five animals by the body parts used for movement, and say how many groups you get. (b) Now group them by whether swimming is recorded for them in Ishita's notes. (c) The duck and the parrot are in the same group in the first grouping. Where does each of them go in the second grouping, and what does this show about grouping?
questions.a: (a) Three groups: legs only - horse, rabbit; legs and wings - parrot, duck; fins - rohu. (b) Swimming recorded - rohu, duck; swimming not recorded - horse, rabbit, parrot. (c) The duck goes with the rohu, while the parrot goes with the horse and the rabbit, so the two are split apart. The group an animal falls in depends on the feature chosen as the basis, so animals can be grouped in various ways.
s: (a) Three groups: horse and rabbit; parrot and duck; rohu
(b) Swimming recorded: rohu and duck; not recorded: horse, rabbit and parrot
(c) Duck joins the rohu and parrot joins the horse and rabbit; the group depends on the feature chosen

questions.q: A school team builds robot animals for a contest. The course has three parts: walk 20 m across grass, get up onto a ledge 3 m high, then walk 5 m along the ledge. Design P copies the goat: it has four legs, walks, and can jump at most 1 m high. Design Q copies the pigeon, but the team gave it wings only. Design R copies the housefly: it has legs and two wings. (i) From the chapter's movement table, give the goat's types of movement and the body part it uses. (ii) What is wrong with Design Q as a copy of the pigeon, and which parts of the course would it fail? (iii) Which part of the course would Design P fail, and why? (iv) Which design should the team enter? Justify it using all three parts of the course. (v) The team may add one kind of body part to Design Q. What should it add, and with which animals of the chapter's table would Q then be grouped by body parts used?
questions.a: (i) The goat walks and jumps, using legs. (ii) The pigeon walks and flies using legs and wings; with wings only, Q cannot walk, so it would fail the 20 m walk across the grass and the 5 m walk along the ledge. (iii) Design P would fail to get onto the ledge: it can jump at most 1 m, the ledge is 3 m high, and it has no wings to fly up. (iv) Design R: its legs let it walk across the grass and along the ledge, and its wings let it fly up the 3 m to the ledge, so it is the only design that can finish all three parts. (v) Add legs; Q would then use legs and wings, which groups it with the pigeon and the housefly.
s: (i) Walks and jumps, using legs
(ii) A pigeon uses legs and wings; Q cannot walk, so it fails both walking parts
(iii) P fails the 3 m ledge: it jumps at most 1 m and has no wings
(iv) Enters R, which can walk (legs) and fly up (wings) for all three parts
(v) Add legs; grouped with the pigeon and the housefly

questions.q:
Class 6 of a lakeside school in Bhopal watches animals at the Upper Lake for one hour. They count 14 fish swimming with fins, 9 egrets walking in the shallow water and flying with legs and wings, 6 cows walking on the grassy bank with legs, and 25 ants walking on a tree trunk with legs. They want to group the animals by the body parts used for movement.
(a) How many animals did they count in all?
(b) How many of the animals use legs in some way?
(c) Group the animals by the body parts used, and give the number of animals in each group.
(d) A visitor says that more than half of the animals counted use legs only. Check the claim with numbers.
questions.a: (a) 14 + 9 + 6 + 25 = 54 animals. (b) Egrets, cows and ants use legs: 9 + 6 + 25 = 40. (c) Fins: fish, 14; legs only: cows and ants, 6 + 25 = 31; legs and wings: egrets, 9. (d) The claim is right: 31 animals use legs only, and half of 54 is 27, so 31 is more than half.
s: (a) Total 54 animals
(b) 40 animals use legs (egrets, cows, ants)
(c) Three groups: fins 14, legs only 31, legs and wings 9
(d) Compares 31 with 27 (half of 54) and accepts the claim

questions.q: What are the special features that enable plants and animals to survive in a particular region called?
questions.a: Adaptations

questions.q: A wildlife photographer has a photo of a camel but has forgotten whether she took it in the cold desert of Ladakh or in the hot desert near Jaisalmer. Which observation from the photo would settle the question?
questions.a: The number of humps on its back: a hot-desert camel has one hump and a cold-desert camel has two. Camels of both deserts have hooves, store food in their humps and live on dry, open land.
o: The number of humps on its back
Whether it has hooves on its feet
Whether it has a hump that stores food
Whether it is standing on dry, open land

questions.q: Match each feature in Column I with the region where it helps the plant or animal survive, in Column II. Column I: 1. Two humps and long hair (camel); 2. Long legs with wide hooves (camel); 3. Conical shape with sloping branches (deodar); 4. Shorter height with smaller leaves (rhododendron). Column II: (a) snowy mountains of Himachal Pradesh; (b) windy mountain tops of the Nilgiris; (c) cold desert of Ladakh; (d) sandy hot desert of Rajasthan.
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: two humps and long hair suit the cold desert of Ladakh, long legs and wide hooves suit the sandy hot desert, the deodar's shape sheds snow, and short rhododendrons with small leaves survive the heavy winds on the Nilgiri mountain tops.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Deodar trees have a flat, wide top so that snow can collect and stay on them.
Reason (R): The mountains in extremely cold regions experience frequent snowfall.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: (a) What are adaptations? (b) Give one adaptation of the rhododendrons on the mountain tops of the Nilgiris and say how it helps them.
questions.a: (a) The special features that enable plants and animals to survive in a particular region. (b) They are of shorter height and have smaller leaves, which help them survive the heavy winds on the mountain tops.
s: (a) Special features that enable plants and animals to survive in a particular region
(b) Shorter height and smaller leaves that help them survive heavy winds

questions.q: True or False: 'The thick, fleshy stems of desert plants such as cactus help them tolerate the hot conditions of the desert.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Very little water is available in deserts; the fleshy stems store water, which helps these plants tolerate the hot conditions.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the fleshy stems store water where very little water is available

questions.q: A transport company has a camel from the hot desert of Rajasthan and a camel from the cold desert of Ladakh, and three jobs. Job 1: carry goods across loose sand dunes near Jaisalmer. Job 2: carry goods along mountain paths in Ladakh. Job 3: stay outdoors through the cold winter of Ladakh. For each job, choose the better camel and name the body feature that decides it.
questions.a: Job 1: the hot-desert camel, whose long legs and wide hooves help it walk on the sand without sinking. Job 2: the cold-desert camel, whose shorter legs let it walk easily in mountainous regions. Job 3: the cold-desert camel, whose long hair from head to neck helps it survive the cold winters of Ladakh.
s: Job 1: hot-desert camel, long legs and wide hooves keep it from sinking in sand
Job 2: cold-desert camel, shorter legs suit mountainous regions
Job 3: cold-desert camel, long hair from head to neck helps in cold winters

questions.q: A herder in Ladakh measures the front hump of his two-humped camel: 30 cm high in October and 18 cm high at the end of February. A tourist says: 'The hump has shrunk by more than half, so the camel must be ill.' (a) By what percentage of its October height did the hump shrink, and is 'more than half' correct? (b) Using the chapter, explain why the humps of a Ladakh camel shrink in late winter. (c) Give your verdict on the tourist's claim that the camel must be ill.
questions.a: (a) It shrank by 30 - 18 = 12 cm, which is 12 / 30 x 100 = 40 percent, so 'more than half' is wrong. (b) Camels store food in their humps. In late winter there is not much food in the cold desert, so the camel uses the food stored in its humps and they shrink. (c) The claim is not supported: shrinking humps in late winter are what the chapter describes for Ladakh camels using their stored food, so the shrinking alone does not show that the camel is ill.
s: (a) 12 / 30 = 40 percent, so 'more than half' is wrong
(b) Little food in the cold desert in late winter, so the camel uses food stored in its humps
(c) Rejects the claim: shrinking in late winter is expected, not a sign of illness by itself

questions.q: Answer each part in one step. (a) Is a river a terrestrial or an aquatic habitat? (b) Is a grassland a terrestrial or an aquatic habitat? (c) What is the habitat of a sea turtle? (d) A frog lives in a pond and also on its muddy bank. What are such animals called? (e) Name any two things that a habitat provides to the plants and animals living in it.
questions.a: (a) Aquatic. (b) Terrestrial. (c) The sea or the ocean. (d) Amphibians. (e) Any two of: food, water, air, shelter.
s: (a) River: aquatic
(b) Grassland: terrestrial
(c) Sea or ocean
(d) Amphibians
(e) Any two of food, water, air and shelter

questions.q:
Ravi has a farmhouse near Bikaner in the Thar desert. On one January day the temperature there was 27 degrees Celsius at 2 p.m. and 4 degrees Celsius at 5 a.m., and it rains on only a few days in the year. He wants to plant a hedge beside the gate. A nursery offers him two kinds of plants: a cactus with thick, fleshy stems, and a deodar sapling with a conical shape and sloping branches. The deodar sapling costs less.
(a) By how many degrees did the temperature fall from the afternoon to the early morning?
(b) Which feature of the cactus suits these conditions, and how does it help?
(c) Which condition is the deodar's shape suited to, and does Bikaner have it?
(d) Should Ravi buy the cheaper deodar? Give a justified decision.
questions.a: (a) 27 - 4 = 23 degrees Celsius. (b) Its fleshy stems store water, which helps it tolerate the hot conditions where very little water is available. (c) Frequent snowfall on cold mountains: the conical shape and sloping branches let snow slide off. Bikaner, a hot desert, does not have frequent snowfall. (d) No. The deodar's adaptation is for shedding snow and does nothing for heat and scarce water, while the cactus's water-storing stem suits a hot desert; paying less for a plant whose features do not suit the region is not a saving.
s: (a) Finds 27 - 4 = 23 degrees
(b) Fleshy stem stores water and helps tolerate heat
(c) Deodar shape sheds snow on cold mountains; Bikaner lacks frequent snowfall
(d) Decides against the deodar, comparing which adaptation suits a hot desert

questions.q: In which year was 'Project Tiger' initiated to protect the declining population of the Bengal Tiger?

In 2022 a newspaper headline read: 'Cheetahs return to India'. The project behind it is called the Cheetah Reintroduction Project, and its aim is to restore the population of the Cheetah. What do the words 'return', 'reintroduction' and 'restore' tell us?
questions.a: Cheetahs once lived in India, but their population had declined.
o: Cheetahs once lived in India, but their population had declined.
Cheetahs are being brought to India for the first time in its history.
The project was set up to protect the Bengal Tiger, as Project Tiger was.
Cheetahs were brought back because their old habitats had grown larger.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the Save Silent Valley Movement?
questions.a: Common people campaigned for 10 years against a dam and saved the forest.
o: Common people campaigned for 10 years against a dam and saved the forest.
The Government began it in 1973 to protect the Bengal Tiger in Kerala.
Local villagers cleared the forest to build a dam across the river.
It was a 2022 project to bring the Cheetah back to the valley.

questions.q: Match each living thing or forest in Column I with the way it is protected, in Column II. Column I: 1. Bengal Tiger; 2. Cheetah; 3. Great Indian Bustard; 4. Sacred grove. Column II: (a) protected by the local community, with no one allowed to cut trees or harm animals; (b) its habitats declared Protected areas in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra; (c) a project initiated to protect its declining population; (d) a project initiated in 2022 to restore its population.
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-b, 4-a: Project Tiger protects the declining Bengal Tiger population, the 2022 Cheetah Reintroduction Project restores the Cheetah, the Great Indian Bustard's habitats are Protected areas in three states, and sacred groves are protected by the local community.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): 'Project Tiger' was initiated in 1973 to protect the declining population of the Bengal Tiger.
Reason (R): The populations of the Bengal Tiger, Cheetah and Great Indian Bustard declined in India mainly because of natural changes in the weather.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: (a) Name the three animals whose populations the chapter says have declined in India. (b) What has caused this decline?
questions.a: (a) The Bengal Tiger, the Cheetah and the Great Indian Bustard. (b) Loss of their natural habitats caused by human activities.
s: (a) Bengal Tiger, Cheetah and Great Indian Bustard
(b) Loss of natural habitats caused by human activities

questions.q: True or False: 'When a habitat is damaged, only the animals living there are affected; the loss of biodiversity does not involve plants.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Damage to the habitats of plants and animals results in the loss of their homes, food and other resources, and this leads to the loss of biodiversity, which includes both plants and animals.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: plants and animals both lose homes, food and resources, leading to loss of biodiversity

questions.q: Compare a sacred grove with Project Tiger. (a) Who protects each of them? (b) Give one way in which their aim is the same.
questions.a: (a) A sacred grove is protected by the local community; Project Tiger was initiated by the Government of India. (b) Both conserve biodiversity: they keep plants and animals safe from the loss of their homes, food and other resources.
s: (a) Sacred grove by the local community; Project Tiger by the Government of India
(b) Both conserve biodiversity by protecting plants and animals and their homes

questions.q: Give three features of sacred groves described in the chapter.
questions.a: Any three: they are undisturbed patches of forest; their sizes vary from quite small to very large; they are found all over India; they are home to different kinds of plants and animals, including many medicinal plants; they are protected by the local community, and no one may harm animals, cut trees or disturb the area.
s: One feature from: undisturbed patches of forest; sizes vary from quite small to very large
A second feature from: found all over India; home to different kinds of plants and animals, including many medicinal plants
A third feature from the lists above or: protected by the local community, and no one may harm animals, cut trees or disturb the area

questions.q: A Protected area of 2,500 hectares of grassland in Rajasthan has been set aside for the Great Indian Bustard. A highway plan would run a new road straight through it, clearing 150 hectares of grassland. A second route goes around the edge of the Protected area and clears no grassland, but it is 18 km longer and costs more to build. (a) Why have such grasslands been declared Protected areas? (b) What percentage of the Protected area would the straight road clear? (c) What would the bustards that use those 150 hectares lose? (d) Which route should the state choose? Give a justified decision.
questions.a: (a) The population of the Great Indian Bustard has declined in India due to loss of natural habitats caused by human activities, so its habitats are protected. (b) 150 / 2,500 x 100 = 6 percent. (c) Their homes, food and other resources in that part of the grassland. (d) The route around the edge. The straight road is shorter and cheaper, but it would cause the same kind of habitat loss that made the bird decline, inside the very area set aside to stop it. The extra 18 km and cost do not damage the bustard's habitat, so the longer route is the better choice.
s: (a) Decline due to loss of natural habitats caused by human activities
(b) 150 out of 2,500 is 6 percent
(c) Homes, food and other resources
(d) Chooses the longer route, weighing distance and cost against habitat loss as the cause of the decline

questions.q:
Students of a school in Mysuru study a lake near their town. In 2015 the lake had 10 km of natural shore, and 150 pairs of a water bird nested along it. By 2025, 4 km of the shore had been filled in for buildings, and only 90 pairs nested there. Now the town plans to fill the rest of the shore for a parking area. The students want to start a campaign like the Save Silent Valley Movement.
(a) What percentage of the shore was filled in, and by what percentage did the number of nesting pairs fall?
(b) Using the chapter, explain why the number of nesting pairs fell.
(c) Name two means the Silent Valley campaigners used that the students could also use.
(d) The town offers to plant 1,000 ornamental trees in a park across town if the parking area is built. Should the students accept? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 4 / 10 x 100 = 40 percent of the shore was filled in; the nesting pairs fell by 150 - 90 = 60, which is 60 / 150 x 100 = 40 percent. (b) Filling the shore damaged the birds' habitat, so they lost their homes, food and other resources, which leads to loss of biodiversity. (c) Any two of: awareness programmes, letters to editors, newspaper articles, seminars, petitions and appeals in court. (d) No. The lake birds need the lake and its shore as their habitat; trees in a distant park do not give them back their nesting places and food, and filling the remaining 6 km of shore would add to the loss already seen (40 percent fewer nesting pairs in ten years).
s: (a) 40 percent of the shore filled; nesting pairs fell by 60, which is 40 percent
(b) Habitat damage meant loss of homes, food and resources, so the birds declined
(c) Two means from the Silent Valley campaign
(d) Rejects the offer: distant trees do not replace the lake habitat, citing the loss so far
